summaries.example: Imagine a friend says, “The library door is open.” You look and see that it is open. The statement matches how things are, so the correspondence view says it is true. If the door is closed, the statement does not match reality and is false.
summaries.summary: The correspondence theory of truth says that a claim is true when it stands in the right relationship to reality. A simple version says that a true claim matches a fact or an obtaining state of affairs. Philosophers have used many words for this relationship, including agreement, representation, and conformity. They have also disagreed about what in reality makes a claim true: it might be a fact, an event, an object, or a property. Some versions focus on whole sentences or propositions. Others explain truth by looking at smaller parts, such as names referring to objects and predicates applying to them. The theory has attracted objections. Critics ask whether facts are mysterious, whether the view is too obvious to count as a theory, and whether we can compare our thoughts with reality without stepping outside our own minds. Competing approaches include coherence, pragmatist, verificationist, deflationary, identity, truthmaker, and pluralist theories.
key_ideas: The correspondence theory says that truth involves a connection between a claim and reality.
Different philosophers describe the connection in different ways, such as matching, representing, or agreeing.
Some versions connect true claims with facts; other versions use states of affairs, objects, events, or properties.
Philosophers disagree about whether every kind of truth, including moral or logical truth, fits this account.
Other theories say truth depends mainly on agreement among beliefs, usefulness, or whether a claim can be verified.
summaries.why_it_matters: Truth affects how we think about learning, language, science, and disagreement. The correspondence theory highlights the idea that the world matters: a belief is not true just because someone likes it or because it fits with other beliefs. Studying this theory also shows why a simple question—“What does it mean for something to be true?”—can lead to deeper questions about facts, language, and how we know things.

important_terms.definition: A statement, belief, or other item that can be true or false.
The idea that a claim is true when it matches something in reality.
Something in reality that helps make a truth true, such as a situation or event.
The world as it is, including objects and what happens to them.

questions_to_think_about: What makes a statement match reality?
Can a statement be true even if nobody believes it?
Could two different statements match the same situation?
Do all kinds of truth need facts in the world?
How could we tell whether a belief matches reality?

summaries.example: Consider the claim, “The package is on the porch.” A fact-based correspondence theory says the claim is true if it corresponds to an obtaining fact or state of affairs involving the package’s being on the porch. A theory that avoids complex facts might analyze the sentence through reference and satisfaction: “the package” refers to an object, and the predicate “is on the porch” is satisfied by that object. These approaches aim at the same truth judgment but explain the connection differently.
summaries.summary: The correspondence theory is best understood as a family of views rather than one single formula. Its central idea is that truth involves a relation to reality. In a narrow fact-based version, a primary truthbearer is true just when it corresponds to a fact; related versions use obtaining states of affairs. The theory must clarify both sides of the relation: what counts as a truthbearer and what kind of reality serves as its correlate. Traditional object-based accounts often rely on subject-predicate structure, which makes it difficult to handle conditionals, disjunctions, and other complex forms. Fact-based accounts avoid that limitation but raise ontological questions about negative, disjunctive, universal, conditional, and other complex facts. Correspondence as isomorphism proposes a structural match between truthbearers and facts, while critics object that this may project linguistic structure onto the world. Logical atomism restricts direct correspondence to elementary truthbearers and handles complex forms recursively. Subatomism goes further by replacing whole-truthbearer correspondence with reference and satisfaction. The entry also distinguishes truthbearers from truthmakers and notes that truthmaker theory may be either a competitor or a broader version of correspondence. Major objections concern the theory’s alleged triviality, its obscure notions of correspondence and fact, its treatment of special domains such as morality and logic, the ‘Big Fact’ argument, and the claim that knowledge would require independent access to reality. The theory’s competitors include coherentist, pragmatist, verificationist, deflationary, identity, and pluralist approaches.
key_ideas: Broadly understood, correspondence theory treats truth as a relational property involving a truthbearer and reality; narrowly understood, it identifies truth with correspondence to a fact.
Object-based versions connect a subject-predicate truthbearer with an object and its properties, while fact-based versions connect a truthbearer with a fact or obtaining state of affairs.

The choice of primary truthbearer matters. Candidates include public sentences, mental representations, and propositions, and theories applied to different kinds of truthbearer need not automatically compete.
Simple fact-based definitions face questions about falsehood, non-obtaining states of affairs, and whether complex truths require complex or ‘funny’ facts.
Logical atomism and subatomism try to avoid assigning a matching fact to every complex truth by explaining complex truth through logical structure or semantic relations.

Competitors—including deflationism, identity theory, truthmaker theory, and pluralism—challenge what correspondence contributes and whether truth should be understood as one uniform relation to reality.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory connects a theory of truth with metaphysics, semantics, logic, and epistemology. It asks whether truth depends on how reality is, rather than only on what we believe, what is useful, or what can be justified. Its internal distinctions also show why apparently simple definitions conceal difficult choices: whether facts exist, whether falsehood requires non-obtaining states of affairs, which entities bear truth, and how linguistic structure relates to the world. Comparing correspondence with its competitors helps clarify what any theory of truth is expected to explain.

important_terms.definition: An item, such as a sentence, proposition, belief-content, or assertion, to which truth or falsity can be attributed.
A relation between a truthbearer and some part of reality, often described as matching, conformity, representation, or agreement.
An item that makes a truthbearer true. In the usual truthmaking use, this need not be a cause.
A fact or state of affairs that obtains; in correspondence theories, it is often proposed as what a true truthbearer corresponds to.
The view that the structure of a true truthbearer and its corresponding fact is similar in a part-by-part or structural way.
A modified approach that explains truth through recursive logical rules grounded in the correspondence of simpler, atomic truthbearers to atomic facts.
An approach that replaces whole-truthbearer correspondence with semantic relations such as reference and satisfaction between constituents and objects.
The view that truth is one property that can be realized in different ways in different domains, with correspondence being only one possible realization.

questions_to_think_about: Does a true sentence need a corresponding fact, or can its truth be explained entirely through reference, satisfaction, and logical structure?
Should a theory of truth allow truebearers that are neither true nor false, or should every truthbearer have one of those two values?
Are facts genuine parts of reality, or are they sentence-like constructions projected from true sentences?
Does the inability to compare a belief directly with mind-independent reality create a serious problem for correspondence theory?
Can correspondence and coherence both contribute to an account of truth without simply becoming competing definitions?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “The science project is in the classroom.” The sentence is true if the project really is there. This sounds simple, but philosophers can explain it in different ways. One might say the sentence corresponds to a fact: the project’s being in the classroom. Another might focus on the words: “the project” refers to an object, while “is in the classroom” is satisfied by that object. Both approaches connect truth with the world, but they disagree about what the important connection is.
summaries.summary: The correspondence theory of truth begins with a familiar thought: a statement is true when it fits reality. Philosophers have expressed this through ideas such as agreement, conformity, representation, and reference. The theory is not one perfectly unified doctrine. Some versions say that a true sentence or proposition corresponds to a fact. Others speak of an obtaining state of affairs, an event, an object, or a property. Historically, object-based theories often analyzed a judgment as having a subject and a predicate connected with an object and one of its properties. Fact-based theories became especially prominent in the twentieth century and were designed to handle truth more generally, including complex sentences. They still face questions about whether reality must contain complicated facts for every complicated truth. Some philosophers respond with logical atomism: only basic claims correspond directly to basic facts, while the truth of complex claims is calculated from their parts. Other approaches move in the opposite direction, explaining truth through smaller semantic relations, such as a name referring to an object and a predicate being satisfied by it. The entry also distinguishes a truthbearer from a truthmaker. A truthmaker is what makes a truth true, but truthmaking is normally not meant to be ordinary causation. Correspondence theory is associated with realism because it emphasizes reality’s role, yet its opponents challenge it in different ways. Coherence theories emphasize fit within a system of beliefs; pragmatist theories connect truth with practical success; deflationists say truth needs less theory; identity theorists say true propositions are facts; and pluralists allow different ways for truth to be realized.
key_ideas: The main correspondence idea is that truth depends on how things are, not only on what people think or agree about.
The theory is a family of views because philosophers disagree about the relation involved and about what part of reality a true claim relates to.
Object-based theories focus on an object and its properties, while fact-based theories focus on facts or states of affairs.
Choosing the truthbearer matters. A theory may apply to sentences, propositions, thoughts, or other items, and these choices affect how complex claims are explained.
Critics worry that correspondence may be too obvious, too mysterious, or unable to explain truths in areas such as morality and logic.
Newer competitors include deflationism, the identity theory, truthmaker theory, and pluralism; some may reject correspondence, while others retain part of its realist motivation.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often disagree not just about particular facts but about what truth itself is. The correspondence theory offers a clear starting point for discussing that disagreement: the world places limits on what can truly be said. Learning its different versions prevents an oversimplified debate between “facts” and “opinions.” It also reveals how questions about truth connect to language, logic, knowledge, and whether reality exists independently of our beliefs.

important_terms.definition: Something that can be described as true or false, such as a sentence, belief-content, statement, or proposition.
A relationship in which a claim agrees with, represents, or matches some part of reality.
Something that makes a truthbearer true; philosophers may propose facts, objects, events, properties, or other items.
A situation that actually exists or occurs. Some theories say true claims correspond to obtaining states of affairs.
A view that true claims are identical with facts, rather than merely related to them.
A theory saying that truth does not need a deep relation to facts; saying that a claim is true can be explained by repeating or endorsing the claim itself.
The view that one idea of truth may be realized by different properties in different areas, such as science and ethics.

questions_to_think_about: If a belief agrees with all your other beliefs but not with what happened, is it true?
What is the difference between a claim matching a fact and a claim being the same thing as a fact?
Can one fact make several different claims true?
Should moral or logical truths correspond to facts, or do they need another explanation?
Does knowing a claim require knowing that it corresponds to reality?
